ashanti-empire.summary: A centralised Akan state that fought four wars against Britain over a century before being annexed.

guru-granth-sahib.summary: Guru Gobind Singh added the ninth Guru's hymns and declared the scripture itself the perpetual Guru, ending the line of human successors.
guru-granth-sahib.note: Sikh tradition regards the text as a living Guru rather than a record of one, which makes "record gap" an imperfect description here.

hume.summary: Showed that causation and the self are habits of mind rather than things observed, a scepticism that woke Kant from his dogmatic slumber.

steam-engine.summary: The first engine that could turn heat into work anywhere, rather than only where a river fell — which is what let factories leave the valleys and cities grow around coal instead of water.
steam-engine.note: The bracket runs from Newcomen's atmospheric engine, which worked but wasted most of its heat, to Watt's separate condenser in commercial production. Watt did not invent the steam engine; he made it efficient enough to put anywhere, which is the part that mattered.

kant.summary: Argued that the mind imposes space, time and causality on experience, and grounded morality in a rule one could will everyone to follow.
kant.significance: He argued the mind supplies the structure of experience rather than merely receiving it, which reframed every philosophical question that followed.

washington.summary: Held a volunteer army together for eight years, then declined to stay in power — twice — which did more to establish how the office would work than anything written down.

lavoisier.summary: Established that matter is conserved in chemical reactions and named oxygen; guillotined during the Terror.

goethe.summary: Wrote the novel that set off the first literary craze in Europe at twenty-four, finished Faust at eighty-two, and did serious work on plant morphology and colour in between.

coal-and-carbon.summary: Burning coal, and later oil and gas, released carbon that had been buried for hundreds of millions of years — the same Carboniferous forests that are elsewhere on this timeline, returned to the air in two centuries.
coal-and-carbon.note: Kept open deliberately. Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 parts per million before industrial coal burning and passed 420 in the 2020s; the line has not turned down, so the entry does not close.

mozart.summary: Toured Europe as a child prodigy, wrote some six hundred works in a life of thirty-five years, and was buried in a common grave.

hokusai.summary: Woodblock prints made cheaply for ordinary buyers in Edo, of which The Great Wave is one — and which, arriving in Europe as packing material, redirected Manet, Degas and Van Gogh.

industrial-revolution.summary: Coal, steam and the factory replaced muscle, water and the workshop, first in British textiles and then almost everywhere — the change that broke the ceiling on how much a population could produce, and began the rise in atmospheric carbon that has not stopped since.
industrial-revolution.note: The end is genuinely disputed. One convention closes the first Industrial Revolution around 1840, after which a Second - steel, chemicals, electricity, the internal combustion engine - runs from roughly 1870 to 1914. Another treats it as one continuous process. The bracket holds both readings rather than choosing, which is why it is unusually wide at the closing end.

american-revolution.summary: Thirteen colonies left the British empire and wrote a constitution on the claim that government derives its authority from the governed — a claim its authors did not extend to the enslaved people many of them owned.
american-revolution.note: The bracket opens at the Stamp Act rather than 1776, because the quarrel that produced the declaration had been running for a decade.

napoleon.summary: Took the French Revolution's army and made himself emperor with it, redrew Europe twice, and left behind a legal code still visible in the law of some seventy countries.

beethoven.summary: Went deaf in his twenties and wrote his late quartets and the Ninth Symphony without being able to hear them, expanding what a symphony was expected to be in the process.

hegel.summary: Saw history as reason working itself out through conflict and resolution, an idea Marx would later turn on its head.

austen.summary: Published anonymously, sold modestly, and turned six novels about marriage settlements among the minor gentry into the standard against which the English novel's handling of irony is still measured.

us-independence.summary: Thirteen British colonies declared themselves free, on the argument that legitimate government rests on consent — an argument whose authors held people in slavery while making it.

romanticism.summary: Feeling, wildness and the individual set against the Enlightenment's order and the factories going up alongside it — the point at which the artist starts being understood as someone with something to express.

bolivar.summary: Led the campaigns that freed six South American countries from Spain, tried to federate them, failed, and died saying that those who serve a revolution plough the sea.

australian-frontier-wars.summary: A century and a half of dispossession and killing as pastoral settlement spread, conducted without treaty and long absent from official histories.
australian-frontier-wars.note: Aboriginal deaths are estimated in the tens of thousands from violence alone, with far greater losses to introduced disease and dispossession. The scale and the framing both remain politically contested in Australia.

image.credit: W.Walton after Louisa and Godfrey Charles Mundy

schopenhauer.summary: Held that a blind striving will underlies everything, and drew openly on Indian philosophy in saying so.

french-revolution.summary: Abolished a monarchy, declared the rights of man, executed the king and then some forty thousand others, and ended with a general in charge — but put popular sovereignty on the table across Europe permanently.

babbage.summary: Designed the Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose mechanical computer with a store, a mill and punched-card programs — a century before one was built, and never finished in his life.

faraday.summary: Discovered electromagnetic induction, the effect that makes every generator and transformer work.

haitian-revolution.summary: The only slave revolt in history to found a state. Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue defeated French, Spanish and British forces in turn, and declared Haiti independent in 1804 — after which France extracted reparations for the loss of its slaves that Haiti paid until 1947.

hawaiian-kingdom.summary: Unified under Kamehameha I and internationally recognised, it was overthrown in 1893 by American business interests backed by US marines — an act for which Congress formally apologised a century later.

vaccination.summary: Jenner's demonstration that cowpox protects against smallpox, building on much older inoculation practice in Asia and Africa.
vaccination.significance: It is the only medical technique that has driven a human disease to extinction, which it did to smallpox in 1980.
vaccination.note: From Jenner's demonstration to national vaccination programmes across Europe and the Americas.

ghalib.summary: The last great poet of Mughal Delhi, who wrote through the destruction of the world he addressed and whose Urdu ghazals are quoted across the subcontinent still.

pushkin.summary: Made Russian a literary language capable of anything, in a career of twenty years ended by a duel at thirty-seven over his wife's reputation.
